newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO warns Serb hardliners, Plavsic meets officers.
newsitem.headline: NATO warns Serb hardliners, Plavsic meets officers.

text.p: NATO countries called on hardliners opposed to Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic on Tuesday to abide by the constitution as the power struggle threatened to produce two rival governments.
NATO leaders meeting in Madrid said Plavsic had acted legally when she dissolved the Bosnian Serb parliament last week and demanded her decisions be respected.
"We will not tolerate any recourse to force or violence, or the unauthorised deployment of military or paramilitary force," an alliance statement said.

NATO officials said Secretary-General Javier Solana discussed the crisis by telephone with Carlos Westendorp, a fellow Spaniard and the international High Representative to Bosnia, earlier on Tuesday.
The confrontation in Bosnia's Serb entity pits Plavsic against fellow nationalists loyal to indicted war criminal and ex-president Radovan Karadzic.
Plavsic has accused Karadzic's circle of plundering Serb terrritory through smuggling rackets and has advocated cooperation with major powers enforcing a peace agreement in Bosnia.

With parliament dissolved, Plavsic will soon have the option of forming a new government and diplomats said two competing authorities in Serb territory could emerge, one in the west and one directed by Karadzic in the east.
The president won promises from Bosnian Serb army generals on Tuesday that they would remain neutral in the conflict after talks in the northwest town of Banja Luka.
The army general staff reiterated its stand that it would not take sides in the feud but respected Plavsic's legal role as supreme commander.
Purged by hardliners and lacking financial support, the army is overshadowed by a well-funded, large police force controlled by Karadzic.
Army sources said the military had nothing to do with a letter broadcast on Serb television over the weekend which attacked Plavsic and alleged she had put Serb territory at risk.
Official Serb media remains under the strict control of Karadzic's deputies and Western envoys have demanded authorities allow Plavsic free access to the television netwrok.
As NATO countries weighed a response to the crisis, U.S. peacekeeping soldiers reported they had seized weapons and ammunition from Bosnian Serb special police loyal to Karadzic.

International police monitors found the unauthorised grenades and other weapons on Monday during an inspection of a special police station in the northern town of Brcko in Serb-controlled territory, U.N. spokesman Alex Ivanko said.

The Serb police initially refused to hand over the weapons to international police but later backed down when American troops from the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) were called in, SFOR said in a statement.

The special police are led by Interior Minister Dragan Kijac who is at the heart of the power struggle. Plavsic precipitated a confrontation with Karadzic and his allies more than a week ago when she tried to suspend Kijac.

No violence has erupted so far in the confrontation between Plavsic, who enjoys support from some police units and soldiers in Banja Luka, and Karadzic's circle based in the mountain village of Pale, outside Sarajevo.

Plavsic dissolved parliament last week and called for new elections on September 1. The hardliners dismissed her decision and held a session of aseembly anyway, rewriting laws to enable her recall and to strip her of defence powers.

The turmoil among Serb leaders has fuelled speculation that major powers are preparing to arrest Karadzic, who was forced out of public office last year as an indicted war criminal but retains covert influence.
